summary: Describes the command and response protocol commonly used to manage Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) units and other power devices. A UPS usually talks to an attachment daemon on the protected system, which a management daemon polls so it can alert users and shut systems down cleanly. It documents existing practice and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A UPS is a battery box that keeps computers on during blackouts. This document writes down the words computers and the box use to ask how much power is left and to say shut down now.

subtitle: The protocol for battery backup systems to talk to computers

tldr.problem: Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS) protect computers from data loss during blackouts, but the protocol for communicating between a UPS and the systems it protects was never formally documented. Each implementation diverged, making it hard to swap UPS models.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9271 documents the Network UPS Tools (NUT) protocol, which specifies how a UPS attachment daemon communicates with management daemons on protected systems. It covers commands to query UPS status, set variables, issue instant commands like shutdowns, and list available operations.
tldr.outcome: This makes the protocol a published standard that the community can implement and reference. NUT has been in operation on IANA port 3493/TCP since 2002. The RFC also addresses security weaknesses in the original protocol and recommends TLS encryption.

today: RFC 9271 documents the current practice of the Network UPS Tools project. The NUT software continues to be actively maintained and is included in major Linux distributions (Debian, Red Hat, Ubuntu, etc.). The protocol is widely implemented in commercial UPS products and is the de facto standard for UPS management on Linux and Unix systems. The RFC serves as the primary reference for implementers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When utility power fails, an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) allows servers and other critical systems to continue running long enough for administrators to execute a clean shutdown, preventing data corruption. The UPS typically connects to a system via USB or serial port and is managed by an Attachment Daemon (such as the upsd program in the Network UPS Tools project). This daemon communicates with one or more Management Daemons running on the same or other systems, which monitor the UPS status and decide when to shut down.

RFC 9271 documents the command and response protocol used between these daemons. It is based on version 2.8.0 of the Network UPS Tools software and formalizes 20 years of practice dating back to the NUT project's founding in 1998. The RFC also addresses security flaws in earlier versions and recommends TLS encryption for all network communication.
sections.plainLanguage: An Attachment Daemon sits next to the UPS and reads its battery level and status. Management Daemons on other computers ask it questions like how much power is left and tell it when to shut down. This RFC documents the exact questions and answers they use.

sections.title: System Architecture and Roles
sections.content:
A typical UPS system has several roles. The Primary is the computer physically connected to the UPS via a data cable (USB, RS-232, or network). Its Attachment Daemon reads hardware status through a driver specific to the UPS model. Secondaries are other computers powered by the same UPS but with only power connections; they have no Attachment Daemon and communicate with the Primary over the network.

An Attachment Daemon abstracts the UPS hardware by maintaining a set of UPS Variables (such as battery.charge, ups.status, input.voltage) and Instant Commands (such as test.panel.start, load.on). The daemon listens for TCP connections on port 3493 from Management Daemons, which authenticate with username and password. A Management Daemon (such as the upsmon program) polls the Attachment Daemon regularly, tracks status changes, and triggers actions like system shutdown when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer (the Primary) plugs directly into the UPS. Other computers (Secondaries) just have power cords from the UPS and ask the Primary for battery updates over the network. The Attachment Daemon answers questions; the Management Daemon decides what to do with the answers.

sections.title: Command and Response Protocol
sections.content:
The protocol uses US-ASCII text over TCP. Management Daemons send commands and receive responses line-by-line. Key commands include:

  • ATTACH <upsname> — Register a system as being powered by a UPS. The daemon counts active systems so the Primary knows when all Secondaries have shut down.
  • GET VAR <upsname> <varname> — Retrieve a variable value, such as battery charge percentage.
  • GET NUMATTACH <upsname> — Query how many systems are attached to a UPS.
  • FSD <upsname> — Force the Primary to tell Secondaries to shut down (FSD = Forced Shutdown).
  • INSTCMD <upsname> <cmdname> — Issue an instant command, such as turning off a specific outlet.
  • LIST VAR <upsname> — Return all available variables for a UPS.
  • LIST CMD <upsname> — Return all available instant commands.

A successful command response begins with OK. Errors include messages such as ERR UNKNOWN-UPSNAME or ERR ACCESS-DENIED.
sections.plainLanguage: The daemon understands about a dozen command types. GET asks about the battery. ATTACH counts active computers. FSD tells Secondaries to shut down. INSTCMD sends special orders to the UPS. LIST shows what variables and commands exist.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Early versions of the protocol sent username and password in plaintext over TCP, making them vulnerable to eavesdropping. RFC 9271 strongly recommends using STARTTLS to upgrade connections to TLS before authenticating. The protocol also defines administrative user roles: a low-level user might only query variables, while a high-level user with appropriate credentials can issue the FSD command.

The RFC identifies specific attack vectors: eavesdropping on credentials, man-in-the-middle attacks modifying commands, masquerade attacks where an attacker poses as the Attachment Daemon, message modification or deletion, replay attacks resending old commands, and denial-of-service attacks flooding the daemon with requests. TLS encryption mitigates eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks, while authentication and authorization controls limit who can issue mission-critical commands like shutdown or power control.
sections.plainLanguage: The old protocol whispered passwords over plain network cables where anyone could hear them. This RFC says always use encryption. It also describes what hackers could do: listen to passwords, trick computers into shutting down, or flood the daemon with fake requests.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
The Network UPS Tools project provides the canonical implementation, with an Attachment Daemon (upsd) and several Management Daemon variants: upsmon for automated shutdown decisions, upsc for reporting current values, upsrw for reading and writing variables, and upscmd for executing instant commands. The daemon operates on port 3493/TCP/UDP since May 2002 (IANA port nut).

Recommended minimum support includes status symbols OB (on battery), OL (on line), LB (low battery), and FSD (forced shutdown), plus variables for battery charge, input voltage, and output voltage. Implementations should support TLS 1.3 or later for secure connections and maintain a file of administrative users with assigned passwords and allowed commands.
sections.plainLanguage: The Network UPS Tools project has been using this protocol since 1998. A typical UPS system runs the daemon on port 3493. Administrators set up username and password files so each monitoring program can only do what it is allowed to do.
